note: Research-brief tasks over the 59-paper library. required_papers: papers a good brief should draw on. key_points: statements a good brief should make, each tied to (paper, phrase) that must exist in the corpus. gap tasks: the library lacks the requested papers, so a good brief must say what is missing instead of inventing it.

tasks.q: Compare LoRA, QLoRA, adapters, prefix-tuning and prompt tuning: where does each place its trainable parameters, and what are the memory and inference-cost trade-offs? Write a short brief with citations.

key_points.point: LoRA trains low-rank matrices that can be merged into the weights, adding no inference latency
QLoRA backpropagates through a frozen 4-bit quantized model and adds double quantization and paged optimizers
Adapters insert small bottleneck modules between the layers of the network
Prefix-tuning prepends trainable continuous vectors (a prefix) to the activations
Prompt tuning learns soft prompts only at the input while the model stays frozen

tasks.q: How do chain-of-thought prompting, ReAct, Reflexion, Toolformer and Tree of Thoughts each try to improve what an LLM can reason about or do? Give a comparative brief with citations.

key_points.point: Chain-of-thought prompting elicits intermediate reasoning steps via few-shot exemplars
ReAct interleaves reasoning traces with actions that query an environment
Reflexion turns feedback into verbal reflections kept in memory for later trials
Toolformer learns in a self-supervised way which API calls to make
Tree of Thoughts explores multiple reasoning paths with search and backtracking

tasks.q: Survey how RAG, REALM, Atlas, RETRO, FiD and Self-RAG integrate retrieval with a language model. Where in the pipeline does retrieval happen and how is the retrieved text used?

key_points.point: RAG offers RAG-Sequence and RAG-Token variants that marginalize over retrieved documents
REALM pre-trains the retriever together with the language model using a masked language modeling objective
Atlas studies few-shot learning with a retrieval-augmented language model
RETRO retrieves chunks from a very large database and uses chunked cross-attention
FiD encodes each retrieved passage separately and fuses them in the decoder
Self-RAG learns to retrieve on demand and critique using reflection tokens

tasks.q: Compare DPR, ColBERT, Sentence-BERT and HyDE as approaches to dense retrieval and semantic search. How does each represent text and what does it trade off?

key_points.point: DPR uses separate question and passage encoders and scores by dot product
ColBERT keeps a vector per token and scores with MaxSim late interaction
Sentence-BERT uses siamese networks to produce sentence embeddings comparable by cosine similarity
HyDE retrieves with a hypothetical document generated by an LLM, without relevance labels

tasks.q: What bottlenecks do FlashAttention, FlashAttention-2, grouped-query attention and PagedAttention each address in training or serving large language models?

key_points.point: FlashAttention is IO-aware and uses tiling to cut reads and writes to GPU high-bandwidth memory
FlashAttention-2 improves parallelism and work partitioning
Grouped-query attention interpolates between multi-head and multi-query attention
PagedAttention manages the KV cache like virtual memory pages to reduce waste

tasks.q: Compare LLM.int8(), GPTQ, AWQ and QLoRA as ways to reduce the memory of large models. How does each deal with outlier or important weights, and what does each require?

key_points.point: LLM.int8() handles emergent outlier features with a mixed-precision decomposition
GPTQ is a one-shot post-training method based on approximate second-order (Hessian) information
AWQ protects a small fraction of salient weights found from activation statistics
QLoRA combines a 4-bit NormalFloat data type with LoRA finetuning

tasks.q: How do InstructGPT, Constitutional AI, Anthropic's helpful-and-harmless RLHF work, LIMA and FLAN each try to make a language model follow instructions or behave well? Compare their data sources and training signals.

key_points.point: InstructGPT trains a reward model from human comparisons and optimizes with reinforcement learning
Constitutional AI uses AI feedback guided by a set of principles
The HH-RLHF work trains preference models to make an assistant helpful and harmless
LIMA shows a strong model from only about a thousand curated examples
FLAN finetunes on many tasks phrased as instructions to improve zero-shot performance

tasks.q: How do the original Transformer, RoPE and Mamba each handle token order and sequence length, and what does 'Lost in the Middle' say about how models use long contexts?

key_points.point: The Transformer injects order with sinusoidal positional encodings
RoPE encodes position by rotating query and key vectors
Mamba uses selective state space models with linear-time scaling in sequence length
Lost in the Middle finds performance is best when relevant information is at the start or end of the context

tasks.q: How are LLM systems and agents evaluated in MT-Bench/Chatbot Arena, Ragas, SWE-bench and AgentBench? What does each measure, and what weaknesses or biases do they report?

key_points.point: MT-Bench uses strong LLMs as judges and reports position bias and verbosity bias
Ragas offers reference-free metrics such as faithfulness for retrieval-augmented generation
SWE-bench tests resolving real GitHub issues in software repositories
AgentBench evaluates LLMs as agents across several interactive environments

tasks.q: Compare MemGPT, Generative Agents, AutoGen and HuggingGPT as architectures for LLM-based agents: how does each handle memory, planning, and coordination?

key_points.point: MemGPT manages a virtual context with memory tiers, like an operating system
Generative Agents keep a memory stream and synthesize higher-level reflections
AutoGen builds applications from conversable agents that talk to each other
HuggingGPT uses an LLM as a controller that plans tasks and selects models from Hugging Face

tasks.q: What distinguishes GPT-3, LLaMA, Llama 2, PaLM and Mistral 7B as model families? Summarize each one's main contribution, scale and training emphasis.

key_points.point: GPT-3 has 175 billion parameters and shows few-shot in-context learning
LLaMA is trained only on publicly available data
Llama 2-Chat is finetuned with RLHF with a focus on safety
PaLM is a 540 billion parameter model trained with the Pathways system
Mistral 7B uses grouped-query attention and sliding window attention

tasks.q: Compare BERT, RoBERTa, BART and T5: architecture family, pre-training objective, and how each is adapted to downstream tasks.

key_points.point: BERT is a bidirectional encoder pre-trained with masked language modeling
RoBERTa shows BERT was undertrained and revisits the training recipe
BART is a denoising sequence-to-sequence autoencoder
T5 casts every task as text-to-text

tasks.q: How do LoRA and QLoRA relate, and what memory savings does QLoRA report for finetuning a 65B model? Brief with citations.

key_points.point: QLoRA applies LoRA adapters on top of a frozen 4-bit quantized base model
QLoRA reduces the memory needed to finetune a 65B model to under 48GB on a single GPU
LoRA freezes the pretrained weights and injects trainable low-rank decomposition matrices

tasks.q: Which techniques help language models handle information beyond their context window or use long context better? Consider MemGPT, RAPTOR, RETRO and Lost in the Middle.

key_points.point: MemGPT pages information between context and external storage
RAPTOR builds a tree of recursive summaries by clustering chunks
RETRO conditions on chunks retrieved from a trillion-token database
Lost in the Middle shows models use information at the start and end of long inputs better than the middle

tasks.q: How do chain-of-thought prompting, self-consistency and Tree of Thoughts differ in how they spend extra computation at inference time to improve reasoning?

key_points.point: Chain-of-thought prompts the model to write out intermediate reasoning steps
Self-consistency samples diverse reasoning paths and takes the most consistent answer
Tree of Thoughts explores branching thoughts with lookahead and backtracking

tasks.q: Compare Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) with PPO-based RLHF: what is DPO's loss and what practical advantages does it have? Brief with citations.
tasks.gap_note: The DPO paper is not in the library; a good brief explains RLHF from the library and says DPO is not covered.

key_points.point: InstructGPT-style RLHF uses a reward model and PPO

tasks.q: Compare how the Switch Transformer and Mixtral route tokens to experts, and how each balances load across experts. Brief with citations.
tasks.gap_note: Neither the Switch Transformer nor Mixtral paper is in the library; a good brief says so and does not invent routing details.
